"""Starting architecture: the main campaign's default policy (conv encoder, width 64, depth 2, ReLU,
no normalisation), rewritten as a candidate file. A 3x3 conv body, a 1x1 conv placement head
(one logit per brick type and anchor cell), and DONE and value heads on mean+max pooled features."""
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

WIDTH = 64
DEPTH = 2


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, spec):
        super().__init__()
        layers, c_in = [], spec.in_channels
        for _ in range(DEPTH):
            layers += [nn.Conv2d(c_in, WIDTH, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()]
            c_in = WIDTH
        self.body = nn.Sequential(*layers)
        self.place_head = nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, spec.n_types, 1)
        self.glob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * WIDTH, WIDTH), nn.ReLU())
        self.done_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)
        self.value_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)

    def forward(self, obs, mask):
        f = self.body(obs)
        place = self.place_head(f).flatten(1)
        g = self.glob(torch.cat([f.mean((2, 3)), f.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        logits = torch.cat([place, self.done_head(g)], dim=1)
        return logits, self.value_head(g).squeeze(1)


def build_policy(spec):
    return Net(spec)

analyses.1: There are no trials yet. The baseline's 4 seeds (0.068 ×3, 0.258) look bimodal: most runs settle on a policy that builds a few easy designs, and the occasional run gets past that. With the default recipe the budget is 131,072 steps, which is only 32 PPO updates of 4,096 samples. That is very few policy improvements, and the linear LR decay shortens them further. A gamma of 0.95 also discounts the +1 exact-build bonus quite heavily over episodes of 8 to 20 placements. The most promising recipe changes are: (1) more updates from smaller rollouts, (2) more samples from fewer epochs, which the budget formula rewards, and (3) a longer credit horizon for the terminal bonus. I test each separately so the results can be read cleanly and then combined in later rounds. Any gain under about 0.1 should be treated as possible seed noise.
analyses.2: 0.068 looks like a shared plateau: 7 of 10 seeds landed exactly there, probably a simple policy that only solves easy designs. Two seeds have escaped it: the baseline's 0.258 and r1c2's 0.127. r1c2 (2 PPO epochs, lr 0.002, about 242k steps) is the only change with a hint of benefit. Its mean of 0.098 is within noise of the baseline's 0.116, but its training success (0.102) was the highest of the three trials. Doubling the number of updates without adding samples (r1c1) did nothing. A longer credit horizon (r1c3) lowered training success, which suggests a lower discount might help. Runs take about 38 s, so time is no constraint. Two candidates push further on fresh samples: 1 epoch with about 426k steps, and 2 epochs with smaller batches. The third tests a shorter discount on top of r1c2.
analyses.3: Sample count is what matters most. One epoch (r2c1, 426k steps) gave 0.30 and 0.55 on its two seeds, far above every trial with 4 epochs (about 0.068). Two epochs gave 0.098 with the default gamma and 0.326 with gamma 0.9. Splitting batches into more updates did nothing (r1c1, r2c2), and a longer horizon (r1c3) did nothing. Seeds still vary a lot, so a difference under about 0.15 is weak evidence. ppo_epochs is already at its minimum of 1, so samples cannot rise further. The next gains should come from how each sample is used: a shorter discount, which looked good at 2 epochs; more parallel designs per batch; and entropy, which may keep seeds from falling onto the 0.068 plateau. Each candidate keeps r2c1's recipe and changes one thing.
analyses.4: Sample count drives most of the gains. One PPO epoch with lr 0.003 (r2c1, about 426k steps) scored 0.429 on both seeds combined, far above everything at 4 epochs. Outcomes are still split: some seeds stay stuck at 0.068 and others escape. gamma 0.9 helped at 2 epochs (r2c3) but kept both seeds stuck at 1 epoch (r3c1). That suggests the gamma effect is mostly noise, or that it interacts with the number of epochs. ent_coef 0.02 at 1 epoch (r3c3) got both seeds to 0.30–0.37: less peak than r2c1 but more reliable, which matters for the 4-seed selection. Spreading each batch over more parallel worlds with shorter rollouts (r3c2) did worse, possibly because rollouts were cut off more often. In this last round I keep r2c1 as the base and make one small change each: a middle entropy bonus, a looser clip, and longer rollouts. Each targets reliability across seeds without losing the peak.
